::: {#def-permutation-p-value}
#### Permutation p-value

With the notation of @def-permutation-distribution,
the **permutation p-value** of the observed statistic $t = T(y)$
is the proportion of relabelings whose statistic is at least as extreme as the observed one:

$$p_{\text{perm}} \eqdef \Pr_\pi\paren{T(y_\pi) \ge T(y)} = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \indic{T(y_\pi) \ge T(y)}.$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-permutation-p-value-lower-bound}
#### A lower bound for the permutation p-value

Because the identity permutation is one of the $n!$ relabelings, $p_{\text{perm}} \ge 1 / n!$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-permutation-p-value}
#### Exact permutation p-value for six expression values

Of the 20 relabelings in @exm-permutation-distribution,
count those whose statistic is at least the observed one.
Rounding before the comparison keeps floating-point error from separating values that are equal in exact arithmetic,
such as the observed statistic and the one for its mirror image:

```{r}
#| label: permutation-p-value-toy
#| code-fold: false
n_extreme <- sum(round(t_toy, 10) >= round(t_observed_toy, 10))
c(
  extreme = n_extreme,
  relabelings = length(t_toy),
  p_perm = n_extreme / length(t_toy)
)
```

The exact permutation p-value is `r n_extreme / length(t_toy)`.
With three samples per group the smallest p-value any data could give is $2 / 20 =$ `r 2 / 20`,
because each statistic has a mirror image, so six samples cannot provide evidence at the 5% level.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-permutation-sharp-null}
#### What a permutation test tests

Relabeling is justified only if the null hypothesis makes the labels irrelevant,
that is, if the two groups have the same distribution.
A permutation test of a difference in means therefore tests the hypothesis of equal distributions.
Such a test can reject because the groups differ in spread rather than in mean,
and a test that does not assume equal distributions needs a different method.
:::
